title: Education Gadfly Weekly: Charter Schools, Ambulance-at-the-Bottom, and Ohio Science of Reading
author: Thomas B. Fordham Institute
source: The Education Gadfly Weekly, Volume 26, Number 33 (fordhaminstitute.org), August 20, 2026
summary: This week's Education Gadfly Weekly, the Thomas B. Fordham Institute's flagship digest, curates three headline commentary pieces plus two research reviews and three ICYMI links, giving Tim a snapshot of the current US K-12 policy conversation. Daniel Buck's lead piece asks whether charter schools, one of the reform era's clearest successes, can survive the spread of universal education savings accounts, arguing charters need deregulation to compete with more nimble private alternatives. Dale Chu's companion piece diagnoses a systemic 'ambulance-at-the-bottom' pattern across reading, math, behavior, and foreign language instruction, where schools wait for problems to become crises rather than intervening early. Aaron Churchill's piece reports on Fordham's own new study of Ohio's science-of-reading implementation, finding real progress in curriculum adoption and teacher training alongside a serious gap: nearly all third graders are still promoted despite most failing the state reading standard, due to a parental-override loophole. The digest's editorial framing, choosing these three pieces together, along with two research reviews on school-quality review processes and early test scores as predictors, and ICYMI links on age-based schooling and charter funding gaps, reflects Fordham's consistent editorial throughline of pairing school-choice advocacy with an evidence-based push for earlier, more rigorous literacy and accountability policy.
points: The digest's curatorial pairing is itself an editorial argument: leading with charter-school competitive pressure (Buck) and systemic underinvestment in early intervention (Chu) frames school choice expansion and early-intervention policy as parallel, related reform priorities rather than separate issues.

Buck's piece surfaces a specific new data point reshaping the choice debate: a survey of 285 charter leaders across Arizona, Florida, and Utah found nearly half report already losing students to ESA-funded private alternatives.

Chu's 'ambulance-at-the-bottom' framing gives a portable diagnostic metaphor, quoting Mitch Daniels's 'dogs don't bark at parked cars,' for why prevention-focused policy is chronically underfunded relative to crisis response across multiple domains of schooling.

Churchill's Ohio piece reveals a specific and stark implementation gap: despite curriculum and teacher-training progress, 98 percent of Ohio third graders were promoted in 2024-25 despite only 61 percent statewide reading proficiency, due to a parental-request promotion loophole.

The FYI section's Emerging Education Policy Scholars program announcement (Fordham/AEI) signals the institute's ongoing investment in shaping the research-to-policy pipeline itself, not just commenting on existing policy.
quotes: Charter schools remain one of the clearest successes of the education reform era, but the rise of vouchers and education savings accounts is changing the competitive landscape. If policymakers want charters to remain a strong public option, they will need to reduce needless regulation and give them room to compete.

Schools too often wait until students are already struggling before they respond, whether in reading, math, behavior, or foreign language instruction. A better approach would ask what needs to happen earlier, and what supports schools need before problems become harder and more expensive to solve.

Fordham's latest report documents the significant work Ohio has undertaken to implement science of reading reforms. But the job isn't done, and the state will need sustained leadership, accountability, and attention to vocabulary and background knowledge if its policies are to translate into higher reading achievement.

New York City tried to broaden school accountability by adding qualitative reviews of instruction, school culture, and improvement systems. New research finds that these reviews may offer useful signals about school quality but produced little evidence of sustained gains in student outcomes on their own.
The Emerging Education Policy Scholars (EEPS) program seeks to counter the long-standing, well-documented divide between research and policy in education.
